Start by trying to wait two hours between cigarettes as often as you can, and you may find yourself surprised how often you can go longer without thinking about it.

One thing I did is I bought a cigarette roller and filters and just rolled my own cigarettes from pouch tobacco (American Spirit, specifically). Only roll them when you want one, and it gives you a time buffer that you can consciously reconsider, or it may just seem like too much of a hassle for something you don't actually need. And on that vein, if you ever say, "I need a cigarette," stop that. You never need a cigarette, you just want one, sometimes really, really badly. You have to be honest with yourself about it.

The longer you can go, the better. The first 3 days are always the hardest, but then your dopamine pathways start to repair.

And breaking down and getting a smoke isn't failure, quitting gets easier every time. I don't even struggle with cravings anymore and can have one or two cigarettes at a party with no cravings the next day, I've probably had four or five packs worth over the last two years.

Obviously it's not a good system for everyone, but it's worked pretty well for me. I like to know I'm in control and that giving in once every month or two doesn't lead me right down the same road.

Or just go cold turkey. If you smoke even a half a pack a day, you can turn that into a pretty nice laptop in a year. Good luck, and Marlboro are the worst, don't smoke those.

I quit nearly a year ago, I guess you could call it "cold turkey" because I haven't had any type of tobacco or nicotine since I made the decision. For the most part this advice does not seem sound.

Do you know what happens when a cigarette addict sets out to go a couple hours without a smoke? It becomes all they can think about, and lighting up becomes a huge relief. This actually reinforces how valuable the cigarette is in their brain. They strengthen their association between tobacco and good feelings - or more accurately, removing the bad feelings.

If someone has made the decision to quit for real, then "breaking down and getting a smoke" IS a failure. It's a huge failure, in fact it's the only possible failure they can make regarding that decision. That first cigarette is the most precious thing in the world to that person, and now they've likely adopted the "I'll never leave you again!" attitude.

Your method may have worked for you, but I'd venture to say that's because you had already made the decision internally to quit when you adopted these ideas and behaviors. For someone who isn't in that mindset, this advice will only strengthen their addiction.

I know it's totally contrary to the "common knowledge" of the twelve step program, but the twelve-step program is hardly a flawless system.

If you're a smoker, you already associate a cigarette with relief. Two hours gives enough time to get the nicotine out of your blood, and starts the process of getting it out of your brain. The more comfortable you are with that duration, the better. It has to be a conscious effort, yes, but saying that smoking once every two hours is worse than smoking once every thirty minutes is really silly.

As far as the "all you can think about" part, it's a matter of time dilation. That part of your brain doesn't have a 2-hour attention span, it's about 3 minutes, and every time you fail to deliver your drug during a craving, you're one step closer to breaking the habit altogether.

Edit: I do want to make it clear that you're absolutely right to challenge my methods. There is no fool-proof solution for addiction, and I'm glad you managed to overcome your own. My mindset was that I didn't hate smoking, I just hated being addicted to it.
